newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia's past hampers investment, official says.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia's past hampers investment, official says.

text.p: Ethiopia's top investment official said on Wednesday a history of famine and civil strife still haunted investments in the Horn of Africa country despite economic reforms and political stability since 1991.

Tadesse Haile, General Manager of the Ethiopian Investment Authority (EIA), told parliament the share of foreign capital in Ethiopia's investments still accounted for only one percent of the total 3,003 investment ventures realised since 1992.
"The low level of foreign investment primarily was due to the long prevailing bad image of the country which used to be associated with civil strife and famine," Tadesse said.
"It will take time to change that image in the eyes of the international community and persuade foreign financiers to invest in Ethiopia," Tadesse told the legislators.
Tadesse said that since an investment proclamation came into force in 1992, foreign financed projects realised in Ethiopia were 29, with gross capital of around $2.3 million.
He added that of the total 1,078 legally registered projects with an aggregate capital of around $9.8 million, 541 had become operational while 537 others were still under construction.

Tadesse blamed bureaucratic hurdles, low level performances and shortages of key services such as electricity, telephones and running water in regions outside the capital Addis Ababa for the delays in project implementation.

Meantime, a corruption scandal reaching Ethiopia's highest political circles is unfolding. State media and government officials are almost silent, feeding the rumour mill since Deputy Prime Minister Tamirat Layne was sacked on October 24.
Privately-owned newspapers are filling the information vacuum. They say Tamirat's downfall has triggered the arrests of numerous and mainly young business tycoons nicknamed "The Bole Millionaires".

Bole is a wealthy suburb in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa favoured by the new rich who have cashed in during the past three years of economic reforms in the formerly Marxist nation of 50 million people.

The private newspapers have named top government and central bank officials as being under arrest or investigation. They claim defence, road construction, sugar and coffee contracts awarded to foreign and local contractors were under scrutiny.
But after weeks of silence, state media reported last week that four top party officials had been dismissed for incompetence and misconduct.

State radio and television said the Oromo People's Democratic Organisation (OPDO) and the Amhara Nation's Democratic Movement (ANDM), both coalition partners of Prime Minister Meles Zenawi's ruling Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPDRF), had each dismissed two of their top officials.
OPDO did not name the sacked officials. The ANDM named its two senior officials sacked from top regional jobs.

When Meles announced the dismissal of Tamirat Layne, his friend and comrade-in-arms during the long struggle to overthrow ex-dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam, he warned other government officials against corruption and abuse of office.
"It is painful to pass such a decision against a close friend. But when the choice is between comradeship and popular confidence, we do not hesitate to take dire action," he said.
